The normalisation of $\boldsymbol v$ makes the target component in \eqref{eq:matched-ridge-response} have conditional variance $\theta^2$ given the background covariates. For each design, we use 500 independent replications for the null $\theta=0$ and for both dense and sparse alternatives at $\theta=0.5,0.75,1$.

The uncentred ridge statistic and the coordinatewise test use a background ridge fit with penalty $0.2n$. The target penalty for the uncentred ridge statistic is one. The MaxCoefT statistic uses a Lasso background fit with the tuning rule in Appendix~\ref{app:experimental-pvalue-conventions}. Both $G$-CRT and the oracle joint CRT use $M=999$ randomised copies, and $G$-CRT uses $L=3$ sweeps. Within each sampler and replication, the two statistics use the same copies. Each test rejects when its p-value is at most $0.05$.

In the settings considered, $G$-CRT achieves power close to the corresponding oracle joint CRTs without knowing the covariate mean or precision matrix. Across all settings in Table~\ref{tab:matched-direct-comparison}, their rejection rates differ by at most $4.4$ percentage points. Under the null, the rejection rates of the four graph-based tests range from $3.8\%$ to $5.8\%$.

In these experiments, $G$-CRT can achieve high power when the coordinatewise test has low power, but this advantage depends on the statistic. For the dense alternatives, $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic is more powerful than the coordinatewise test in design B, whereas the ordering is reversed in design A. Replacing the uncentred ridge statistic with MaxCoefT increases the power of $G$-CRT in design A but reduces it in design B. These patterns hold at each of the three signal strengths considered. For example, at $\theta=0.75$, $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic has a rejection rate of $75.8\%$ in design B, compared with $10.0\%$ for the coordinatewise test. In design A, the corresponding rates are $39.6\%$ and $82.8\%$, respectively. For the sparse alternatives, $G$-CRT with MaxCoefT is more powerful than both the coordinatewise test and $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic in both designs.

To quantify the individual conditional effects, let $\mathbf\Omega=\mathbf\Sigma^{-1}$, and let $\beta_j$ be the coefficient of target $j$ in \eqref{eq:matched-ridge-response}. Since $1/\Omega_{jj}=\operatorname{Var}(X_j\mid\boldsymbol X_{-j})$, the part of the response signal that remains after conditioning on all covariates other than target $j$ has standard deviation $|\beta_j|/\sqrt{\Omega_{jj}}$. We measure this signal relative to the noise and account for sample size through $\sqrt n|\beta_j|/(\sigma\sqrt{\Omega_{jj}})$, where $\sigma=1$ is the noise standard deviation. For example, at $\theta=0.75$, these effects range from $3.514$ to $3.722$ in design A and from $0.934$ to $1.198$ in design B, while the conditional signal variance of the target group is $0.5625$ in both designs. Thus, at the same group signal strength, design B provides much less signal for detecting an individual conditional effect. This is consistent with the low power of the coordinatewise test and $G$-CRT with MaxCoefT in B, alongside the higher power of $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic, which uses the overall improvement in fit.

For the dense alternative at $\theta=0.75$, we numerically approximate the expectations in \eqref{gcrtb:eq:population} using the background covariate samples from the 500 replications in each design. The target contribution gives a larger positive difference between the observed and randomised gains in design B than in design A. Its interaction with the remaining background contribution further increases this difference in B and reduces it in A. Together, the two terms give leading approximations of $0.0408$ in A and $0.0945$ in B for the observed gain minus a randomised gain. Thus, the leading calculation places the observed gain further above the randomised gains in B, providing a possible explanation for the higher rejection rate of $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic: $75.8\%$ in B compared with $39.6\%$ in A, despite the same group signal strength.

The combined test draws on both statistics without selecting one in advance. Across the alternatives considered, its rejection rate exceeds that of the less powerful component, while it is lower than that of the more powerful component in some settings and higher in others. The Bonferroni adjustment imposes a stricter threshold on each p-value, while allowing either component to trigger rejection. For example, in design B at $\theta=0.75$, the combined test has a rejection rate of $70.0\%$ under the dense alternative, compared with $75.8\%$ for $G$-CRT with the uncentred ridge statistic. Under the sparse alternative, its rejection rate is $87.0\%$, compared with $81.2\%$ for $G$-CRT with MaxCoefT. Relative to the more powerful component in each setting, these are a decrease and an increase of $5.8$ percentage points, with paired Monte Carlo standard errors of $1.1$ and $1.4$ percentage points, respectively.

We examine whether vector centring reduces the sensitivity of $G$-CRT power to the sign of the background contribution, with the conditional target signal held fixed. The experiment extends the comparisons in Appendix~\ref{app:centering-simulation} to conditionally dependent targets and more background variables than observations. We use $n=80$ observations, $t=8$ target variables and $s=112$ background variables. Let $\mathbf\Theta$ be the $8\times8$ tridiagonal matrix with diagonal entries one and adjacent entries $-0.2$, and define $\mathbf V=\mathbf\Theta^{-1}$. Define $\lambda_*=1-0.4\cos(\pi/9)$ and the unit vector $\bs v\in\mathbb R^8$ by $v_j=\sqrt{2/9}\sin(j\pi/9)$, $j=1,\ldots,8$, so $\mathbf\Theta\bs v=\lambda_*\bs v$. Independently for each $i=1,\ldots,n$, generate mutually independent $\bs S_i\sim \mathcal{N}_{112}(0,\mathbf I_{112})$, $\bs E_i\sim \mathcal{N}_8(0,\mathbf V)$ and $\varepsilon_i\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$. For each $b\in\{-1,1\}$ and $r\in\{0,0.15,0.30,0.60\}$, use
\bs X_{i,\mathcal T}=0.5\bs v S_{i1}+\bs E_i,\qquad
Y_i=(b-0.5r\sqrt{\lambda_*})S_{i1}+r\sqrt{\lambda_*}\bs X_{i,\mathcal T}^\top\bs v+\varepsilon_i.

With conditionally dependent targets, the residual score vectors of the copies can retain part of the target signal after these scans. The matrix $\mathbf F$ in \eqref{gcrtint:eq:scan} describes this retention: in the leading approximations \eqref{gcrtb:eq:observed-score-approximation} and \eqref{gcrtb:eq:randomised-score-approximation}, it maps the target signal contribution for the observation to that for each copy. For this graph and scan order, $\|\mathbf F\|_{\mathbf\Theta}\approx0.0598$, so each copy retains at most about $6\%$ of the observed target signal contribution in the norm induced by $\mathbf\Theta$. Thus, even with $L=1$, the difference between the leading target signal contributions retains most of the observed signal.

We compare three $G$-CRT tests using the residual score vectors and regularised residual Gram matrices in \eqref{gcrtcent:eq:residual-scores}. One test uses the uncentred gain $\bs c_v^\top\mathbf D_v^{-1}\bs c_v$, which yields the same candidate ordering as the uncentred ridge statistic by \eqref{gcrtb:eq:rank}. The other two use the symmetrically centred ridge residual scores in \eqref{eq:symmetric-centered-statistic}, with $\mathbf W=\mathbf D_{\rm pool}^{-1}$ for the inverse pooled Gram weight and $\mathbf W=\mathbf I_8$ for unit weight. The background penalty is $0.2n$, the target penalty is $\lambda_n=1$, and the intercept is unpenalised. For each test, we calculate the conservative p-value from unrounded scores by \eqref{eq:crt-pvalue-conservative} and reject when $p\leq0.05$.

All methods use the same perturbed response in each replication and refit their background models. The covariate matrix, graph and target set remain fixed. We use 400 replications at each noise level, with the same seed for corresponding replications across levels.

Figure~\ref{fig: stock noise} in Section~\ref{sec: fund} presents the empirical detection rates across the five noise levels. The $G$-CRT with LM-L1-R-SSR has the highest empirical detection rate among the four CRT procedures at all five noise levels, tied with dCRT (L1) at the lowest noise level. For example, at $\sigma=0.10$, its detection rate is $94.3\%$, compared with $72.8\%$ for dCRT (L1). Both tests based on linear models have higher detection rates than the two tests based on random forests throughout the examined range. Detection rates generally decline as noise increases; dCRT (RF) rises from $31.5\%$ at $\sigma=0.05$ to $35.0\%$ at $\sigma=0.10$ before declining.

The likelihood ratio test compares the unpenalised multinomial logistic models using $\bs{X}_{\mc{S}}$ alone and using both $\bs{X}_{\mc{S}}$ and $\bs{X}_{\mc{T}}$. Its p-value uses the asymptotic chi-squared reference distribution with $18(K-1)$ degrees of freedom, where $K$ is the number of observed response categories. Some fits exhibit separation, so we compute the log-likelihood suprema even when finite maximum likelihood estimates do not exist. For both the observed data and all 400 simulated datasets, we verify the log-likelihood values using lower and upper bounds with a gap of at most $10^{-5}$.

This gives a p-value of approximately $9.58\times10^{-6}$. In the simulation under conditional independence reported in Table~\ref{tab:appendix BCR type 1}, however, the test rejects in $40.0\%$ of replications at the nominal $5\%$ level. We use the $G$-CRT to avoid relying on the chi-squared approximation.

We run 400 replications with $\mc S$ and $\mc T$ fixed. When a simulated response omits a category, we use the observed number of categories to determine the LRT degrees of freedom and omit unused category levels from the RF fit. All four methods yield p-values in all 400 replications. This simulation does not repeat probe selection or the inverse normal transformation and does not establish validity of the p-value obtained after selection in the original analysis.

Figure~\ref{fig: BCR pvalue lrt} shows an excess of small LRT p-values, indicating that the chi-squared approximation is inaccurate in this setting. The rejection rates of the three CRTs are much closer to the nominal level.
On the observed data, the p-values are $0.018$, $0.697$, and $0.407$ for $G$-CRT with the RF statistic, dCRT (L1), and dCRT (RF), respectively.

At the $5\%$ level, the $G$-CRT rejects the joint null, whereas neither coordinatewise dCRT does. Its rejection rate under the fitted null is much closer to the nominal level than that of the likelihood ratio test. The differences in the observed p-values also reflect the treatment of the response categories and the scoring methods.
